transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-10 15:30 UTC | Duration ~62m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (NimbleSearch Head of Search), Jenny Lopez (ML Eng), Mark Wu (Infra), Eli Torres (PM)
Links shared: benchmark spreadsheet (https://redwood.example/benchmarks/nimble-3-10), security whitepaper (https://redwood.example/security/soc2.pdf)

00:00 Speaker 1 (Alex): hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick agenda — deep dive on embeddings and reranking perf and cost, priya will lead the perf stuff, i'll cover pricing and next steps
00:18 Speaker 2 (Priya): cool hi Samir, Jenny, Mark — quick question to start, what's your current embedding dim and candidate set size in production?
00:30 Speaker 3 (Samir): yeah right now we're using 384 dims from an open model, candidate set is about 500 on initial retrieval then top 100 for rerank, p95 latency target for rerank is 200ms today
00:45 Speaker 2 (Priya): got it — and what's your throughput? qps at peak?
00:50 Speaker 3 (Samir): peak is around 120 qps, but bursty, and we have nightly batch adds too. cost is a big concern — we pay to host vectors + inference costs, so curious where we can trade latency for cost
01:12 Speaker 1 (Alex): yeah cost/latency tradeoff is core. two levers: model size/emb dim and batching/caching strategy, plus runtime improvements like quantization. priya?
01:30 Speaker 2 (Priya): right — quick high level: smaller dims reduce compute and memory linearly-ish, e.g., 128 vs 384 is roughly 3x fewer FLOPs for the dense op, but you often see quality drop depending on dataset. quantization (int8/int4) helps reduce memory and increase throughput on GPU but can introduce small accuracy shifts.
01:55 Speaker 4 (Jenny): question — for rerank we do a small cross-encoder on the topk (like 100), how does batching interact with that? we need latency under 200ms for p95 ideally
02:10 Speaker 2 (Priya): batching helps GPU utilization. if you have 120 qps and you batch candidates across queries you can get much better throughput, but batching increases tail latency unless you have strict SLOs and smart batching (latency-aware batching). we recommend dynamic batching with max batch latency threshold (e.g., 10-20ms) to keep p95 down. also use prefix/KV caching for the query encoding part — if portions of the context are reused, KV cache avoids recompute.
02:40 Speaker 5 (Mark): can you explain KV cache memory behavior? we're concerned about GPU memory with 1536-dim embeddings when we go larger
02:50 Speaker 2 (Priya): sure — KV cache size scales with seq length and hidden size; for decoder models kv is per-token keys/values. for embeddings/rerank it's more about storing vectors in memory for similarity search. on the runtime side our serving runtime keeps KV in GPU memory for fast autoregressive workloads; for rerank we typically keep dense vectors in CPU memory or vector DB (Pinecone/FAISS) and use GPU for scoring. if you want to do in-GPU dense dot products at low latency you need to ensure GPU memory has capacity — quantization can reduce that footprint. also, our runtime supports sharding vectors across GPUs to fit larger corpora.
03:25 Speaker 3 (Samir): for us candidate scoring is the bottleneck — we do a dot product for all 100 candidates per query, multiply by machine count. is there an approach where you precompute some stuff to reduce per-query cost?
03:40 Speaker 2 (Priya): yes, precompute static parts — e.g., document embeddings are precomputed. for rerank with cross-encoders you can't precompute cross-attention, but you can use two-stage approaches: lightweight bi-encoder for initial scoring followed by cross-encoder on top-k. Also caching topk retrievals for repeated queries can help. our platform supports a local prefix cache on the worker to keep frequently accessed vectors hot.
04:05 Speaker 4 (Jenny): curious about quantization — we've tried int8 and saw weird drops, do you have numbers?
04:15 Speaker 2 (Priya): empirically, int8 usually has ~0-1% nDCG drop on retrieval tasks for many models, int4 more variable, maybe 1-3% depending on model. but you should run evals on your dev set. the big win is memory and throughput — int8 halves memory vs fp16 and can allow larger batch sizes or more shards per GPU. also mixed-precision kernels and optimized GEMM give throughput boosts.
05:00 Speaker 1 (Alex): linking to the benchmark sheet — we ran sample tests with dims 128/384/1536 on T4-like and A100-like GPUs, and saw cost per 1000 queries change drastically. i'll share that sheet after the call.
05:20 Speaker 3 (Samir): ok good — can you speak to p95 numbers? our SLA is p95 rerank <= 200ms and embedding generation <= 50ms for interactive features
05:35 Speaker 2 (Priya): on an A10/A100 class machine with optimized kernels, for 384-dim embeddings we saw p50 ~12-18ms and p95 ~35-60ms for single request embedding generation (no batching). For rerank (100 candidates) using a bi-encoder scoring on GPU with int8 we saw p50 ~40-60ms, p95 ~120-180ms depending on batching and contention. with strict latency SLOs you might use dedicated capacity to avoid noisy neighbors.
06:10 Speaker 5 (Mark): dedicated capacity — what are the tradeoffs vs hosted? we prefer VPC with private endpoints or fully on-prem because of compliance
06:20 Speaker 1 (Alex): Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools, predictable latency and isolation; Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you the control plane locally and egress restrictions. tradeoff is operational overhead and higher committed cost. we can run pilot in your VPC with our private control plane, or provide an on-prem bundle if needed.
06:50 Speaker 4 (Jenny): how does batching affect p95 for rerank when you have bursty traffic?
07:00 Speaker 2 (Priya): burstiness is tough — dynamic batching with adaptive timeouts helps, and request shaping at the gateway level can smooth bursts. if you need <200ms p95 under bursts, either keep small max batch sizes (e.g., 8-16) or scale out more workers. Also consider asynchronous reranking for non-blocking flows.
07:30 Speaker 3 (Samir): cost math — can you walk through an example? say 120 qps, 100 candidates, 384-d embeddings, running on A100s with int8 quantization
07:45 Speaker 1 (Alex): sure rough calc: assume per-query end-to-end cost = embedding cost + scoring cost. embeddings at 40ms on A100 might be X tokens cost, scoring 100 dot products on GPU amortized via batching could be Y. in our sheet we show cost per 1000 queries for that profile around $Z (we'll put exact numbers in the sheet). main levers to reduce cost: lower dim, better batching, quantization, or move scoring to CPU vector DB for cheaper but slightly higher latency.
08:30 Speaker 5 (Mark): if we move scoring to CPU/FAISS, what's the latency hit for 100 candidates?
08:40 Speaker 2 (Priya): depends on hardware. optimized CPU AVX builds can do tens of thousands of ops per second; for 100 candidates you might still be in the 50-120ms range but it's variable. GPUs shine for large batch scoring. Also consider hybrid: do nearest neighbor on CPU then GPU for top N.
09:05 Speaker 4 (Jenny): we also want to keep model quality. any recommended dim for semantic search? we started on 384 but wondered if 256 or 1536 is better
09:20 Speaker 2 (Priya): 384 is a good sweet spot for many general-purpose models. 128 is lightweight but may lose fine-grained signal; 1536 increases quality but costs more. recommendation: run an ablation on your nDCG/L2 recall with 128/256/384 and one large variant like 1536; often 384->1536 gains are diminishing for many datasets.
09:45 Speaker 3 (Samir): ok we can run that. can Redwood run the benchmarks in your infra or do you want us to run locally?
09:55 Speaker 1 (Alex): we can do both. we recommend running in your VPC for realistic networking and storage; we can also run a controlled benchmark in our hosted infra to compare. either way Priya will provide the runner and scripts.
10:12 Speaker 6 (Eli): security question — if we go private/VPC, how is keys/crypto handled?
10:20 Speaker 1 (Alex): we integrate with KMS/HSM for key management, support customer-managed keys, SOC 2 audit logs, RBAC, SAML/SSO — we'll share the security pack.
10:35 Speaker 5 (Mark): networking: can the workers be pinned to subnets with no internet egress? that's a requirement
10:42 Speaker 1 (Alex): yes, with Private deployments we can operate in completely restricted subnets; the control plane can be customer-managed and we support egress controls. we'll need specifics from Mark to validate drivers and NACLs.
11:00 Speaker 2 (Priya): back to perf — practical benchmark plan: 1) run embedding generation latency for dims [128,256,384,1536] at varying batch sizes [1,4,8,32], capture p50/p95 and throughput; 2) run rerank flow: initial retrieval (CPU or vector DB) + GPU scoring on top-100, measure end-to-end p50/p95 and cost per 1000 queries; 3) evaluate quantization int8 and int4 impact on nDCG and latencies; 4) test with simulated bursty traffic to observe p95 behavior.
11:40 Speaker 4 (Jenny): timeline?
11:45 Speaker 1 (Alex): we'll aim to have initial benchmarks by 2026-03-17, cost model and pricing by 2026-03-12, and a VPC pilot plan by 2026-03-20.
12:00 Speaker 3 (Samir): great — one last question: what about KV cache warmup and cold start behavior? We saw big p95 spikes after deploys
12:12 Speaker 2 (Priya): cold starts are common. our runtime does background warming: prefetch popular vectors into GPU memory and keep a LRU for evictions. for cross-encoder rerank, warming is less helpful since cross-attention can't be precomputed, but for embeddings/bi-encoder scoring you can pre-warm the vector cache. Also rolling restarts and staged rollouts reduce full-cold windows.
12:45 Speaker 5 (Mark): any gotchas for on-prem hardware variations? we plan to use our own servers with A10s and some older T4s
12:55 Speaker 2 (Priya): older cards like T4 have lower throughput; quantization helps. kernel selection matters — we test for each card type. we can provide suggested instance shapes and shard counts for your corpus size.
13:15 Speaker 1 (Alex): ok wrapping up — recap and next steps: Priya runs benchmarks, Alex shares cost sheet and pricing, customer provides queries and constraints, schedule VPC pilot planning. we'll capture outcomes in the benchmark doc and follow up next week.
13:40 Speaker 3 (Samir): thanks everyone, looking forward to results
13:45 Speaker 1 (Alex): thanks all, we'll follow up with notes and artifacts

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard words (e.g., "A ten" vs "A10" show up). There was some crosstalk around 02:40–03:00.

End of transcript.
